title: From WHAT to HOW: How Cognitive Science Transformed My Lesson Plans
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher describes how studying cognitive science moved her lesson planning from asking what content and activities to cover to asking how students will actually learn it. She works through ten HOW questions, each with a stated cognitive-science rationale and a concrete application to a single lesson on global beef demand and Amazon deforestation. The questions cover chunking, activating prior knowledge, building a schema, sustaining attention, rehearsal, checking for understanding, scaffolds and models, processing, making expert thinking visible, and planning in-the-moment adaptation. The argument is that these principles, drawn from Rosenshine, cognitive load theory and Sherrington, add purpose and precision rather than extra workload. The piece works as a practical translation of research into a planning routine.
points: The central shift is from content-focused to cognition-focused planning: the question moves from what to teach to how students will encode it.
Each planning question is paired with a cognitive-science rationale, such as limited working memory behind chunking and rehearsal behind retrieval.
The single worked example (beef demand and deforestation) shows how a cause-effect schema can be built and revised across a lesson.
Planning for pivots in advance, such as a simplified diagram or a think-pair-share, makes adaptation a designed part of the lesson.
The author argues the HOW questions do not add workload but give structure to work teachers already do.
quotes: When I used to plan lessons, my focus was mostly on the what: what content I’d cover, what standards I needed to hit, what activity students would do. But after diving deep into the science of learning and cognitive science over the past year, something fundamental shifted.
Cognitive load theory tells us that working memory is limited. If we overload students, retention drops. Chunking helps manage that load and build understanding step-by-step.
New learning connects best when it hooks onto existing knowledge. Without that connection, students struggle to make sense of it or retain it.
Attention is a gatekeeper to learning. If I don’t keep students mentally engaged, the information doesn’t get encoded in the first place.
Rehearsal is how we encode information. It strengthens memory traces and makes retrieval easier later.
If I don’t know what students are thinking, I can’t support them. Checks for understanding help guide what happens next.
Experts don’t just know more. They think differently. Making that thinking visible helps students learn how to approach a problem or concept.
